paragraphs.text: Some of the most impressive buildings of the ancient world are still standing nearly two thousand years after they were built. The dome of the Pantheon in Rome, completed around 125 AD, remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome on Earth. Harbour walls built by Roman engineers along the Mediterranean coast have survived centuries of constant attack by seawater. Modern concrete, by comparison, often begins to crack and crumble within fifty to a hundred years, particularly in marine environments.

For a long time, the durability of Roman concrete was attributed mainly to its ingredients. Roman builders mixed lime with volcanic ash, known as pozzolana, which was found in large quantities near the Bay of Naples. When this mixture reacts with water, it forms extremely stable minerals. The Roman writer Vitruvius, whose ten-volume work on architecture is the only such text to survive from the period, recommended specific proportions of lime and ash, and much research has focused on reproducing his recipes.

A study published in 2017 added an unexpected element to the story. Researchers at the University of Utah examined samples from Roman harbour structures and found that seawater, far from damaging the concrete, had actually strengthened it. As seawater seeped through tiny cracks, it dissolved some of the volcanic material and allowed new crystals of a rare mineral, aluminous tobermorite, to grow. These crystals filled the gaps and bound the material more tightly together. Producing this mineral in a laboratory requires very high temperatures, yet in the harbour walls it had formed slowly at the temperature of the sea.

In 2023, a team led by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology proposed a second explanation. They had noticed small white lumps of lime scattered through samples of Roman concrete. These had previously been regarded as evidence of poor mixing or low-quality materials. The team concluded instead that they were the result of a technique called hot mixing, in which quicklime, rather than lime that had already been combined with water, was added directly to the mix. The chemical reaction produces considerable heat, which speeds up the setting process and leaves behind lumps of lime that remain chemically active.

These lumps, the researchers argued, give the concrete the ability to repair itself. When a crack forms and water enters, it dissolves some of the lime, which then reacts to form calcium carbonate and seals the crack. To test the idea, the team produced samples of concrete using both ancient and modern methods, deliberately cracked them and ran water through them. Within two weeks, the cracks in the hot-mixed samples had closed completely, while water continued to flow through the samples made with modern methods.

The findings have attracted interest from the construction industry, which is responsible for around 8% of global carbon dioxide emissions, much of it from the production of cement. Concrete that lasts longer would need to be replaced less often, reducing emissions over time. However, Roman techniques cannot simply be copied. Roman concrete is considerably weaker than modern concrete when it is first poured and takes longer to set, which makes it unsuitable for many modern purposes, such as tall buildings. Engineers are therefore exploring ways of adding self-healing properties to modern mixes rather than returning to ancient ones.
